summary.text: Chemical equilibrium is the state in which reactants and products are both present in concentrations that have no further tendency to change with time.
It results when the forward reaction runs at the same rate as the reverse reaction; those rates are generally not zero, just equal.
Because both reactions keep going with no net change in concentrations, this state is known as dynamic equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: What equilibrium is
paragraphs.text: Chemical equilibrium is the point in a reaction where the amounts of reactants and products present no longer tend to change over time. Looking from outside, you would see no change in the properties of the system. This state is what the field of equilibrium chemistry studies.

paragraphs.heading: Still busy underneath
paragraphs.text: Equilibrium does not mean the reaction has stopped. The forward reaction and the reverse reaction both keep going, usually at rates above zero. They simply run at the same rate, so the concentrations show no net change. That is why the state is called a dynamic equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: Left or right
paragraphs.text: Chemists describe where a reaction settles with a simple picture. If nearly all the reactants have been used up once the balance is reached, the equilibrium lies far to the right. If hardly any product has formed, it lies far to the left.

paragraphs.heading: One number for the balance
paragraphs.text: The balance can be summed up by an equilibrium constant, which arises as a ratio of the forward and reverse rate constants, with the products written on top by convention. This constant stays the same whatever the amounts of the substances involved, though it does change with temperature. Equal forward and reverse rates are a necessary condition for equilibrium. On their own, though, they do not explain why equilibrium happens.

paragraphs.heading: Catalysts and disturbances
paragraphs.text: A catalyst speeds up the forward and the reverse reaction in the same way. It helps the system reach equilibrium sooner, but it leaves the equilibrium constant untouched. Changing the conditions is a different matter. Le Châtelier's principle, from 1884, predicts that a disturbed equilibrium shifts its position so as to partly undo the change.

paragraphs.heading: The energy view
paragraphs.text: At constant temperature and pressure, the quantity to watch is the Gibbs free energy, G, which then depends only on the extent of reaction, written ξ. The second law of thermodynamics allows G only to fall as the reaction runs, and at equilibrium G stops changing as ξ changes. Mixing products with reactants adds a large amount of entropy, which gives the Gibbs energy a distinct minimum along the way. If the reactants and products were completely pure, sitting in separate regions of space, there would be no reversibility and no equilibrium.

paragraphs.heading: A proton on the move
paragraphs.text: Acetic acid in water gives a small picture of this constant traffic. A proton can hop from one acetic acid molecule onto a water molecule, then onto an acetate ion, forming a fresh acetic acid molecule. The number of acetic acid molecules ends up unchanged, even though the proton has moved. This is dynamic equilibrium at the scale of single molecules.
